summary:
Afghanistan under the Taliban presents the most extreme risk to a transgender visitor of any jurisdiction documented here. The EUAA COI Report of February 2026 finds no legal protection on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity either before or after the 2021 takeover, and records Amnesty International's position that same-sex relations are punishable by death.

Criminalisation runs in two layers. The Human Dignity Trust country profile, updated 19 January 2026, states that Afghanistan criminalises same-sex sexual activity between men and between women: Penal Code 2017 provisions on sodomy and inciting sodomy carry up to two years' imprisonment, while the Code's Sharia-reference clause permits the death penalty for same-sex activity. The Taliban's Promotion of Virtue and Prevention of Vice Law of 31 July 2024 adds a preventive surveillance duty. Its Article 22 obliges regime overseers to intervene against listed evils including lesbianism and homosexuality "even if with one's own spouse", placing same-sex conduct under continuous moral supervision alongside adultery and gambling.

Enforcement is documented as systematic and violent. Human Rights Watch and OutRight, reporting 26 January 2022 on 60 interviews with LGBT Afghans, found Taliban members and their supporters attacking, threatening and expelling LGBT people from their homes, with family, neighbour and partner abuse surging after the takeover. OutRight's own report of 14 February 2023, based on 22 interviews with LGBTIQ Afghans still in the country, found security officials pursuing gay men and trans women more systematically than in the early months of rule, using physical and sexual assault, arbitrary detention and public flogging for alleged same-sex relations; the Taliban Supreme Court has confirmed such punishments on social media. CNN reported in November 2024 first-person accounts of arbitrary detention, beatings and sexual abuse in Taliban custody as the crackdown intensified.

Public corporal punishment has expanded. UN human-rights experts condemned the Taliban's use of it in an OHCHR press release of March 2026, recording at least 1,110 people flogged in 2025 alone, nearly double the 2024 figure, and warning that women, girls and LGBT+ people face heightened punishment for moral crimes including adultery, illicit relationships and sodomy.

Marriage and partnership recognition are absent in both eras. Under the Islamic Republic the 1971 Law of Marriages required a legal marriage between two Muslim adults of the opposite sex, with Article 41 directing that gaps be resolved through Islamic law principles, and the 1949 Law on Marriages, Weddings and Circumcision likewise framed marriage as between a Muslim man and a woman; no same-sex marriage, civil union or domestic partnership was recognised. Under Taliban rule since 2021, same-sex relationships and marriages are not recognised at all.

A JURIST feature of 8 November 2024, drawing on the Rainbow Organization of Afghanistan formed by Afghan LGBTQ refugees, reports systematic persecution after August 2021, notes that even the post-2001 constitution provided no protective framework, and identifies visibly transgender individuals as facing the gravest risks including exploitation and violence. DW's feature of 2 October 2021 profiles a trans man and a gay friend hiding in Kabul, stating that under Taliban rule LGBTQ people face the death penalty and their only option is to leave, and documents street attacks on men coded as gay, who changed their clothing and confined themselves indoors.
tangentialFactors:
Afghanistan's LGBTIQ population sits at the centre of the European Union's asylum assessment for the country. The EUAA Country Guidance, section 3.17, profile last updated January 2023 and carried into guidance in May 2024, treats LGBTIQ Afghans as persons perceived to transgress religious and social norms, in the same protective category as minors without support networks and persons facing the death penalty; this is the framework under which Afghan LGBTIQ protection claims are examined in the EU.

International accountability mechanisms have begun to register the persecution. On 23 January 2025 the ICC Prosecutor, Karim Ahmad Khan, requested arrest warrants against Taliban leaders Hibatullah Akhundzada and Abdul Hakim Haqqani for the persecution of women, girls and the LGBTQ community, the first time that court has recognised crimes against the LGBTQ community.

The comparative baseline is unfavourable rather than mixed. The previous government offered no anti-discrimination protection either: no law addressed discrimination or harassment on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, political parties were prohibited from advocating anything opposing Islamic morality, and the 2017 and 2020 US State Department reports recorded that organisations defending LGBTI freedom remained underground because they could not legally register with the government. Persons convicted of homosexuality under the Islamic Republic were generally sentenced to prison in the cities, so urban residence carried a defined judicial outcome rather than the arbitrary enforcement reported since 2021.
localsOnly:
Healthcare access is constrained by law, stigma and limited infrastructure. The 2017 US State Department report found that LGBTI community members did not have access to certain health services and could be fired from jobs because of sexual orientation. Before 2003 little or no HIV-AIDS education or treatment existed; the 2008 official count stood at 504 people living with HIV-AIDS, though the true figure was suspected to be in the thousands. The first HIV-AIDS treatment centre opened in Kabul in 2009 with more clinics promised, access to anti-retroviral drugs is at best limited, and the 2020 report states that the government permits condom distribution only to married couples, excluding same-sex couples, alongside documented stigma against people living with HIV. Low literacy, weak infrastructure and social taboos impede comprehensive public health education.

The penal code carries provisions that reach into ordinary family and caregiving situations. Article 430 made it an Instigation of Delinquency for an adult to promote or assist a minor in adultery, homosexuality or prostitution, a clause that can capture any caregiver or partner in a same-sex household, and Article 427 increased punishment where the victim was under 18. Article 398 offered lesser punishment for vigilante honour killings that can target minors found engaging in homosexuality, and Article 373 imposes fines or murder-equivalent penalties for spreading a dangerous disease. Under the Islamic Republic, young victims of sexual exploitation were often charged rather than the adult perpetrators.

Youth are a documented target. Bacha bazi involves teenage boys kidnapped, dressed in women's clothing, made to dance in competitions and forced into sexual acts; militia members without access to women kidnap boys to be humiliated and raped, other boys become prostitutes regardless of sexual orientation, and the practice was reported in 2007 as still common in northern Afghanistan. Armed faction commanders kidnapped, trafficked and raped young boys after 2001 without action being taken by the US Department of Defense or the Afghan government despite awareness. A former president signed an agreement to ban the practice and a law prohibited Afghan soldiers from having their ashna live with them, but enforcement was rare and police were reportedly complicit. When the Taliban came to power in 1996 they banned bacha bazi alongside homosexuality, both carrying the death penalty. Article 430 can deter adults from seeking care for minors by treating any adult who promotes or assists minors in adultery, homosexuality or prostitution as committing Instigation of Delinquency.

Public education on sexual orientation and gender identity is restricted. Beyond low literacy and social taboos, censorship provisions apply: Article 32 of the 2002 Press Law prohibits incitement to depravity and Article 27(D) of the 1973 Postal Law bars material repugnant to public decency. Hamid Zaher's 2009 memoir about growing up gay in Afghanistan, It Is Your Enemy Who Is Dock-Tailed, cannot be distributed within the country. A 2011 survey found young men displaying rainbow symbols without knowing their meaning and quickly removing them, and the 2017 and 2020 State Department reports noted that awareness of sexual orientation or gender identity remained limited and homosexuality was widely seen as taboo.
outOfScopeNotes:
Entry and visa screening are not addressed by the available sources. No source in this inventory describes passport checks, questioning at airports or land borders, or any screening that could disclose a visitor's gender identity or trans status on arrival, so entry-side exposure remains unresolved.

Rules on gender markers in identity documents, and whether a foreign passport bearing a marker inconsistent with the holder's presentation would attract attention at inspection, are likewise not sourced here and should be treated as unresolved.

The practical application of the death penalty for same-sex activity since 2021 is unresolved. The Human Dignity Trust profile establishes that the Sharia-reference clause permits it and Amnesty International is cited for the position that same-sex relations are punishable by death, but no source in this inventory records a completed execution for that offence under the current authorities; the OHCHR figures for 2025 record floggings rather than executions.

Enforcement data post-dating March 2026, and any reporting on how the morality-law surveillance duty in Article 22 is applied to foreign nationals or visitors as distinct from residents, is not covered by these sources.

Consular protection, the availability of emergency exit routes, and whether any government advises against travel on the basis of LGBTIQ status are outside the inventory and remain unverified.
